source.title_on_document: Inquiry-based learning in STEM education: the impact of generative AI-based Chatbots on primary school students' problem posing ability in science

supplement.where: Additional files 1 and 2, online version at https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-026-00631-0 (p. 19, Supplementary Information)
supplement.holds: Additional file 1: final versions of problem posing Tests 1 and 2 (p. 9). Additional file 2: baseline (pre-test) between-group tests, within-group pre-post paired t-tests, and ENA visualizations of baseline and within-group change (p. 13). The post-test between-group statistics are in the main text (Table 5).

paper_design_summary: Two intact third-grade classes (97 students) in one primary school in central China; one class was randomly selected to use a custom GenAI chatbot (Question Pot, GLM-4) and the other the Baidu search engine during three problem-based inquiry lessons on the 'Air' unit. Students' problem posing was scored on a 15-minute paper-and-pencil test before and after the intervention (number, category, quality, and total score, coded by two researchers), and in-class question records were analyzed with epistemic network analysis. Cognitive load and technology acceptance were self-reported.

studies.label: Class-level comparison of GenAI chatbot vs search engine in third-grade science inquiry (problem posing)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Technology tool used in the problem-based inquiry lessons: GenAI chatbot (Question Pot) vs Baidu search engine, assigned to whole classes
assignment.quote: One class was randomly selected as the experimental group (N = 48), and the other as the control group (N = 49), with technology conditions allocated at the class level.
assignment.locator: p. 5, Methods, Participants; also p. 1, Abstract ('randomly assigned by class'); the paper calls the design quasi-experimental

arms.name: Experimental group (chatbot)
arms.description: Used the custom GenAI chatbot 'Question Pot' (GLM-4 on the ChatGLM platform) on tablets in three problem-based inquiry lessons, in multi-round dialogue to generate and refine questions

arms.name: Control group (search engine)
arms.description: Used the Baidu search engine on tablets in the same three problem-based inquiry lessons, relying on text-based retrieval and reading to develop questions

participants.exclusions: 185 test papers collected. Pre-test baseline used 90 valid samples (46 experimental, 44 control). Post-test and within-group analyses kept only students with complete pre- and post-test participation: 89 (45 experimental, 44 control), so 8 of 97 assigned students dropped (3 experimental, 5 control); reasons beyond the pairing rule are not given. Questionnaires: 93 collected, 7 excluded for missing data or straightlining, 86 analyzed (42 experimental, 44 control). Randomization was of two classes, one per arm.
participants.who: Third-grade primary school students aged 8-9, two classes in one school
participants.quote: The final number of valid samples included in the analyses was 89 (45 in the experimental group and 44 in the control group).
participants.locator: p. 5, Participants (97 students, 48/49); p. 12, Data analysis (90, 89, 86); p. 13, Table 5 (N = 89)

ai_tool.name_model: Question Pot, a custom agent built on the ChatGLM platform using the GLM-4 model
ai_tool.how_used: Students held multi-round dialogues with a researcher-configured chatbot during the inquiry lessons. The bot taught questioning strategies, offered progressive prompting ideas based on students' initial questions, and showed example questions; follow-up suggestions were on in Topic 1 and disabled in Topics 2-3 to stop copying; a 'Smart Star' motivational mechanism was added in Topics 2-3 (p. 8, Table 2). Tablets were used only in the problem-based inquiry lessons; the pre- and post-tests were paper tests (p. 6, Fig. 1; p. 12).

task.description: Science problem posing: students posed as many questions as they could (questions only, no answers) about three short text or text-and-image science contexts (Test 2: air movement forms wind, air can be compressed, applications of air in daily life); during the intervention, students posed questions in three thematic inquiry lessons with the assigned tool
task.duration: 15 min per test; intervention of three thematic inquiry topics, each with several regular lessons and one problem-based inquiry lesson (total calendar length not stated)

outcomes.name: Post-test total problem posing ability score
outcomes.question: after_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Composite out of 10 = number (max 3) + category (max 2) + quality (max 5), computed from questions coded by two trained researchers (Kappa 0.886 on pilot, 0.827 on 20 percent of study data; discrepancies resolved by discussion). Formulas (1)-(4) on p. 11. Not labeled creativity by the paper; the dimensions draw on fluency/flexibility/originality frameworks (p. 4).
outcomes.delay: Not stated. Problem posing ability test 2 was given in the post-test stage after the three inquiry topics (p. 6, Fig. 1).

contrasts.reported: Total Score: experimental M 5.80 (SD 0.59, N = 45) vs control M 5.36 (SD 0.73, N = 44); t = 3.07, df = 82.61 (adjusted), p = 0.003, Cohen's d = 0.65
contrasts.locator: p. 13, Table 5; p. 13, Results RQ1 text; p. 1, Abstract

outcomes.name: Post-test question quality (Bloom cognitive level) score
outcomes.question: after_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Each question coded on a five-level revised-Bloom scale (R=1 remembering/understanding, P=2 applying, A=3 analyzing, E=4 evaluating, C=5 creating); student score is the weighted average normalized to a 0-5 range (p. 10, Table 3; p. 11, Eq. 4). The paper says the scale considers 'complexity, novelty, and uniqueness' (p. 11).
outcomes.delay: Not stated. Post-test after the three inquiry topics (p. 6, Fig. 1).

contrasts.reported: Quality: experimental M 2.46 (SD 0.26, N = 45) vs control M 2.29 (SD 0.35, N = 44); t = 2.47, df = 87, p = 0.015, Cohen's d = 0.52

outcomes.name: Post-test number of questions (level score)
outcomes.question: after_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Count of valid interrogative questions posed in 15 minutes, binned into five levels (L1 <= 5, L2 6-10, L3 11-15, L4 16-20, L5 >= 20) and scored L x 0.6 (max 3) (p. 10, Table 3; p. 11, Eq. 2). Raw counts are not reported.
outcomes.delay: Not stated. Post-test after the three inquiry topics (p. 6, Fig. 1).

contrasts.reported: Number: experimental M 2.12 (SD 0.57, N = 45) vs control M 1.92 (SD 0.65, N = 44); t = 1.52, df = 87, p = 0.132, Cohen's d = 0.32

outcomes.name: Post-test question category score
outcomes.question: after_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Each question coded into one of six categories with point values (IQ irrelevant 0, SC context-based 1, SL learned knowledge 2, SR real-life 3, OD other-discipline 1, CQ comprehensive 2); student score is the weighted average x 2/3 (max 2) (p. 10, Table 3; p. 11, Eq. 3). It is a weighted average of category values, not a count of distinct categories.
outcomes.delay: Not stated. Post-test after the three inquiry topics (p. 6, Fig. 1).

contrasts.reported: Category: experimental M 1.22 (SD 0.15, N = 45) vs control M 1.15 (SD 0.24, N = 44); t = 1.76, df = 73.72 (adjusted), p = 0.082, Cohen's d = 0.38

outcomes.name: Post-test epistemic network structure (category x quality code co-occurrence)
outcomes.question: after_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Epistemic network analysis on 11 researcher-assigned codes (6 category, 5 quality) from post-test questions; group mean networks and a subtracted network, visual comparison only (epistemicnetwork.org). Unit of the ENA model is not stated.
outcomes.delay: Not stated. Post-test after the three inquiry topics.

contrasts.reported: No statistics. Subtracted network: stronger experimental connections around SL, SR, P, and E; stronger control connections around R (R-SC, R-P). No group formed stable connections to the 'creating' node.
contrasts.locator: p. 13, Results RQ2; p. 14, Fig. 3; p. 17, Discussion

outcomes.name: In-lesson epistemic network structure across inquiry Topics 1-3
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: ENA on category and quality codes of questions from Question Pot dialogue records and Baidu search records during the three inquiry lessons; mean networks and centroid trajectories per topic and group; quantity not coded and ability scores not computed for this phase (p. 11; p. 12). Visual comparison only.

contrasts.reported: No statistics. Experimental network expanded and deepened across topics with more nodes participating; control network showed localized changes in connection strength with node count unchanged.

company_involvement.description: No company involvement stated. The chatbot was built by the researchers on the ChatGLM platform (GLM-4); funding from National Natural Science Foundation of China and Fundamental Research Funds for the Central Universities; authors declare no competing interests.

eligibility.reason: Criterion 1: the condition was randomized between two intact classes (one class per arm), and the paper itself calls the design quasi-experimental; with a single cluster per arm the tool contrast is confounded with class, so this may belong with quasi_people/observational rather than core. The comparison is chatbot vs search engine (ai_vs_active). Criterion 2: 89 students analyzed (45 vs 44), 97 assigned. Criterion 3: outputs are open-ended science questions scored by researchers on number (fluency), category, and Bloom-level quality; only the number dimension maps to a coded creativity construct, and the task is problem posing rather than a task judged on novelty or creativity, so fit with the creativity scope is a judgment call. All scored test outcomes were produced without AI (after_ai, paper post-test).

one_line_finding: On a paper post-test taken without AI, third-graders whose class used a GenAI chatbot during inquiry lessons scored higher than the search-engine class on total problem posing ability (5.80 vs 5.36, t = 3.07, p = 0.003, d = 0.65) and question quality (2.46 vs 2.29, p = 0.015, d = 0.52), with no significant differences in number or category (p. 13, Table 5).
open_questions: Does randomization of the tool between two intact classes (one per arm, self-described quasi-experiment) satisfy criterion 1, or should it be coded quasi_people?
Is science problem posing scored on number, category, and Bloom-level quality inside the creativity scope? Only 'number' maps to fluency.

Timing: the post-test came after the three inquiry topics in a separate stage; the gap from the last chatbot lesson is not stated. Coded immediate with after_ai because AI was not available during the post-test.
notes: Self-reported outcomes not listed as outcomes because they are not scored on output: cognitive load (mental load, mental effort, overall; higher = lower load; experimental 4.59 vs control 4.17 overall, t = 2.41, p = 0.018, n = 42 vs 44; p. 14, Fig. 5) and technology acceptance (overall 5.27 vs 4.75, t = 3.09, p = 0.003; p. 15, Fig. 6). Baseline equivalence (no significant pre-test differences, p > 0.05) and within-group pre-post tests are only summarized in the text; statistics are in Additional file 2, not in this PDF. 3010 coded question entries across all phases (p. 12); not split by phase or arm. The comparison arm is a search engine, so there is no no-aid control.
